transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi. Well, I came in because... I just can't seem to stop worrying once it starts. It could be about anything, really—like my mother getting up at night, or a grant report, or just wondering if I missed something at work. 

Once the thought is there, I can’t seem to, you know, shelve it in my mind. No matter how many lists I make or how hard I try to redirect myself to something else, the worry just stays there and I can't control it.
Do you ever experience thoughts that feel intrusive or unwanted, that bother you because they don’t align with who you feel you are or what you believe?

No, I don't think so. I mean, the worries are unwanted in the sense that I'm exhausted by them and wish they would stop, but they don't feel strange or against who I am. They're just normal, everyday concerns—like about the library or my family—that I just can't let go of. So, no, I haven't noticed any thoughts that feel like they go against my beliefs or anything like that.
Have these worries been connected to a specific stressful event or change in your life recently?
Yes, actually. This has all been going on for about a year and two months now. That’s when my mother had a fall and had to move into my home with me. So, it definitely started with that change.
Do the worries continue even when you’re not actively thinking about the stressor, like your mother’s fall or the changes in your life since then?

Yes, they definitely do. Over this past year, my worrying has really spread out. It started with just worrying about my mother's safety, but now... it's about finances, staff decisions at the library, deadlines, the house, and just wondering if I’m being a good daughter. It feels like even the small things can start to feel like they’re about to unravel, even when I'm not directly thinking about my mother moving in.
Have you noticed any physical symptoms, like restlessness, feeling on edge, fatigue, or muscle tension, that seem to go along with these worries?

Yes, definitely. I feel a lot of tension in my muscles. By the time the evening comes around, my neck and shoulders just feel completely locked up. I think I spend most of the day just bracing myself. And I've noticed I clench my jaw a lot, too—especially when I'm working on emails or just sitting there listening to hear if my mother needs me in the next room.

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms have persisted beyond the expected duration of an adjustment disorder (which typically resolves within 6 months of the stressor). The spread of worries to multiple domains, associated physical symptoms (muscle tension, jaw clenching, feeling on edge), and persistence of symptoms for over a year align more strongly with Generalized Anxiety Disorder. No features of other disorders have been endorsed.
